prompt.context: C.M. Burns Manufacturing Co. is a $20B annual revenue consumer electronics company that has just purchased Smithers Electronics, a $4B annual revenue consumer electronics company. Both companies spend a significant amount of money on branding and marketing their different products. Both are present in all major channels, and both produce DVDs and Blu-Ray players, televisions, MP3 devices, and headphones. Products are not differentiated in terms of quality or functionality, but branding sets them apart and distinct customer segments prefer one brand to the other. Both are US-based firms with operations in the US and both exist in all major channels across the US. Product mix is the same, meaning each company generates the same proportion of revenues from each product category. Both manufacture proprietary goods with their own operations. Both sell products via retailers; neither sells direct. Growth of each company is stable.
prompt.question: The CEO of Burns, Charles Montgomery Burns, has come to your firm to request help identifying $350M in near-term synergies in order to justify the stock-price premium that Burns Manufacturing paid for the acquisition of Smithers. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any revenue synergies available from cross-selling or bundling?
clarifying_info.a: Both companies have the same product mix and serve distinct brand-loyal customer segments. Revenue synergies are not expected to be a significant opportunity here.

clarifying_info.q: Is there opportunity to eliminate one brand?
clarifying_info.a: No — distinct customer segments prefer each brand, so both brands must be maintained.

clarifying_info.q: Are there opportunities to consolidate manufacturing or distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Labor and distribution are already optimized; there is not a lot of room for improvement in those areas in the near term.

clarifying_info.q: What is the geographic footprint of each company?
clarifying_info.a: Both are US-based with operations in the US, present in all major channels.

clarifying_info.q: Are there long-term supplier contracts in place?
clarifying_info.a: That is a risk to consider — contract terms would need to be examined.

exhibits.title: Cost Categories Across Each Company

framework: Recognize that revenue synergies are unlikely: same product mix, brand-differentiated segments — focus exclusively on cost synergies
Identify cost categories from Exhibit 1 and prioritize by size and tractability
Key insight: CM Burns revenues are 5X those of Smithers ($20B vs $4B) — costs that are proportional to volume (components, packaging) should reflect this ratio at Smithers, enabling a price benchmark
Apply 5X revenue multiplier to determine where Smithers' costs should be vs. where they are, yielding realizable savings
Components: highest priority (largest absolute gap vs. 5X benchmark) — renegotiate Smithers' supplier contracts to match CM Burns' per-unit pricing
Packaging: second priority — same logic, smaller but meaningful savings
Marketing: not cuttable — brands must be maintained to preserve distinct customer segments
Labor/Distribution: already optimized, not actionable near-term
Overhead: apply multiplier math but challenge feasibility — costs may not be proportional to revenue volume, so savings may not be realizable near-term
Quantify total near-term savings and compare to $350M target
Identify long-term synergies (distribution, overhead, labor) and next steps

questions.prompt: What cost categories should we prioritize for near-term synergies, and why?
questions.guidance: Strong answer immediately focuses on cost synergies (not revenue synergies) because product mix is identical and brand differentiation precludes easy revenue uplift. Candidate should note the 5X revenue ratio ($20B vs $4B) and recognize that variable/volume-driven costs (components, packaging) should scale with the revenue ratio — where Smithers pays more per unit than the 5X benchmark implies, there is a negotiating opportunity. Marketing cannot be cut easily as it supports brand differentiation. Labor and distribution are stated as already optimized.

questions.prompt: Using the components cost data, calculate the savings available if Smithers' component costs are renegotiated to match CM Burns' per-unit pricing.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the 5X multiplier: CM Burns cost / 5 = where Smithers cost should be. Savings = Smithers current cost minus the implied benchmark. Sum across sub-categories.

math.setup: CM Burns revenues are 5X Smithers revenues. If supplier pricing per unit is the same, Smithers costs should be 1/5 of CM Burns costs. Savings = Smithers_current - (CM_Burns / 5).
steps: Molded plastic: CM Burns $600M / 5 = $120M benchmark. Smithers current = $200M. Savings = $200M - $120M = $80M
Chips/processors: CM Burns $800M / 5 = $160M benchmark. Smithers current = $200M. Savings = $200M - $160M = $40M
Metal casing: CM Burns $1,200M / 5 = $240M benchmark. Smithers current = $400M. Savings = $400M - $240M = $160M

questions.prompt: Using the packaging cost data, calculate the savings available if Smithers' packaging costs are renegotiated to match CM Burns' per-unit pricing.
questions.guidance: Same 5X multiplier approach. Note that recycled materials/cardboard cannot be compared between the two companies (different category labels), so no savings are assumed there.

math.setup: Same 5X benchmark logic. Savings = Smithers_current - (CM_Burns_equivalent / 5). Cardboard/recycled materials categories are not comparable — excluded.
steps: Styrofoam: CM Burns $160M / 5 = $32M benchmark. Smithers current = $80M. Savings = $80M - $32M = $48M
Plastic: CM Burns $690M / 5 = $138M benchmark. Smithers current = $160M. Savings = $160M - $138M = $22M
Cardboard (CM Burns) vs Recycled materials (Smithers): not comparable — no savings assumed

questions.prompt: Do total near-term savings reach the $350M target?
questions.guidance: Components ($280M) + Packaging ($70M) = $350M exactly, meeting the target. Candidate should state this clearly and note the precision is somewhat coincidental but the logic holds.

questions.prompt: What overhead savings might be available, and are they realizable?
questions.guidance: Applying the 5X multiplier to overhead: Salaried staff — CM Burns $200M / 5 = $40M benchmark, Smithers current $120M, implied savings $80M. IT — CM Burns $1,400M / 5 = $280M benchmark, Smithers current $280M, savings $0M. However, overhead costs are not necessarily proportional to revenue volume (unlike components and packaging), so the 5X benchmark may not apply. These savings are not realizable in the near term without more information.

math.setup: Apply 5X multiplier to overhead sub-categories, then assess feasibility.
steps: Salaried staff: $200M / 5 = $40M benchmark. Smithers current = $120M. Math implies $80M savings, but overhead may not scale with revenue.
Conclusion: overhead savings are not reliably realizable in the near term.
math.answer: Not realizable near-term; overhead does not necessarily scale with revenue volume

brainstorming.prompt: Now that we have identified $350M in near-term synergies, what long-term synergies might the combined company pursue?

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Economies of scale from combined volume should allow distribution costs to fall below the current 5-to-1 ratio
Consolidate logistics networks and carrier contracts across both companies

categories.name: Overhead / IT
ideas: Consolidate separate IT systems into a single platform over time
Streamline corporate functions (finance, HR, legal) to eliminate duplication

categories.name: Labor / Operations
ideas: Bring manufacturing operations together over time to remove excess capacity
Labor costs on a per-unit basis should decrease as combined production is rationalized

recommendation: Re-negotiate supplier contracts for Smithers Electronics so that raw material costs align with CM Burns' per-unit pricing
Components renegotiation yields $280M in savings; packaging renegotiation yields $70M in savings — totaling exactly $350M and meeting the acquisition justification target
risks: Long-term supplier contracts may limit ability to renegotiate in the near term
Analysis assumes same level of quality between suppliers and goods across the two companies — quality differences would invalidate the benchmark
next_steps: Examine existing supplier contract terms to determine if renegotiation is feasible (long-term lock-ins?)
Identify relevant Smithers suppliers and initiate outreach with new deal terms benchmarked to CM Burns pricing
Commission a long-term study of additional synergies available from distribution, overhead consolidation, and labor optimization
